docs.title: Banking Delta Lakehouse
docs.text:
Daily pipeline: MySQL, MongoDB and Databricks public → PySpark → PostgreSQL (landing → staging → analytics → marts) → Databricks Delta. Airflow orchestrates, stored procedures transform, and SQL data-quality suites gate every layer.

Start here Quickstart — run the project locally Blueprint Architecture — layers, flow, gates, contracts Day to day Runbook · Troubleshooting Business findings Insights

This site is built from main and served at the GitHub Pages root. Branch previews live under /preview/<branch>/ (dev, staging, qa) and carry a noindex tag so they stay out of search engines.

docs.title: Airflow — Banking-Delta-Lakehouse
docs.text:
Airflow 3.3.2 (CeleryExecutor) in Docker Compose orchestrates the daily run. It contains no pipeline logic: every task calls the same scripts and SQL as python main.py (docs/PIPELINE.md). Two DAGs live in airflow/dags/.

Colour legend: docs/PIPELINE.md (violet = Airflow services, indigo = pipeline steps run inside the worker, slate = audit, red = gates/failures, yellow = mail).

docs.title: Environment split (easy to get wrong)
docs.text:
File Loaded by Holds airflow/.env.airflow docker compose --env-file .env.airflow (interpolation) and every container (env_file:) AIRFLOW_VERSION, PYTHON_VERSION, image tag, DB/Redis settings, pipeline secrets (PG_*, MYSQL_*, MONGO_*, DATABRICKS_*, SMTP_*)

environment: in docker-compose.yml beats env_file: for the same key, so ENVIRONMENT (default development) and GIT_SHA (set by make up to the local HEAD, -dirty when uncommitted) always come from the compose file; shell or CI exports win over both. Copy .env.airflow.example → .env.airflow and fill it in. Missing AIRFLOW_VERSION makes docker compose config fail immediately. docker-compose.dev.yml bind-mounts code, sets DAGS_ARE_PAUSED_AT_CREATION=false and adds host.docker.internal so containers can reach services on the host.

# from the repo root (GIT_SHA = local HEAD, ENVIRONMENT defaults to development)
make up
make down
# or from airflow/ with the explicit env file (always include the dev override):
cd airflow
cp .env.airflow.example .env.airflow          # fill secrets
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml \
  --env-file .env.airflow up airflow-init     # must exit 0
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml \
  --env-file .env.airflow up -d
# UI: http://127.0.0.1:8080 (login from .env.airflow)

docs.title: Summary task states, env and build
docs.text:
summary.collect_task_states() merges three sources in order: audit.table_runs (pipeline truth — SKIPPED means no data past the watermark, and it wins), context["task_states"] (Airflow 2 only, absent in Airflow 3) and the Airflow 3 Task SDK (ti.get_task_states(dag_id=…, run_ids=[run_id]) through the supervisor, never the metadata DB). Step durations come from ti.get_task_breadcrumbs. A core step with no state renders UNKNOWN and banners [UNKNOWN], never NOT_RUN and never a false green; the notes then list how many states were unavailable.

env= and build= in the mail and the report come from the container environment: compose passes ENVIRONMENT (default development, set it explicitly outside development) and GIT_SHA. make up exports the local HEAD (-dirty when uncommitted); CI should export GIT_SHA=$GITHUB_SHA. The report prefers the GIT_SHA environment variable and falls back to .git/HEAD on the host. Check a running stack with:

docker compose -f airflow/docker-compose.yml --env-file airflow/.env.airflow \
  exec airflow-scheduler env | grep -E 'ENVIRONMENT|GIT_SHA'

docs.title: Architecture — Banking-Delta-Lakehouse
docs.text:
The blueprint of the project. Read this first; AGENTS.md holds the rules for working in the repo, and docs/*.md drill into each subsystem. If this file and the code disagree, the code wins — then fix this file.

Banking-Delta-Lakehouse is a daily lakehouse pipeline: three source systems are landed into PostgreSQL with PySpark, transformed by SQL stored procedures through four layers (raw → staging → analytics → marts), gated by data-quality suites at every step, and finally published to Databricks Delta where a read-only dashboard serves them. Airflow schedules it; main.py runs the identical steps by hand.

docs.title: 2. Design principles
docs.text:
1. One way to run the pipeline. main.py and the Airflow DAG call the same scripts and the same SQL. Airflow adds scheduling, retries, pools and alerting — it contains no pipeline logic of its own (airflow/dags/banking_delta_daily.py).
  2. Gate before the next layer. A failing step stops the run; a critical data-quality failure blocks publish. Nothing downstream ever reads a half-loaded layer.
  3. Idempotent by construction. Every load is safe to run twice with the same input.
  4. Watermarks move only with the data. A watermark advances inside the same transaction as the write, so a crash never loses or double-counts rows.
  5. Audit survives failure. Audit rows are written in their own short transactions; the DQ gate COMMITs its verdict before it RAISEs.
  6. Correct types. Money is NUMERIC(18,2) / Decimal, never float. All instants are timezone-aware UTC; Spark JVM + SQL session run in UTC.
  7. Layer ownership is strict. Each schema is written by exactly one owner (see §5).
  8. Hermetic by default. CI and the local gate need nothing external; anything that touches real data or credentials is scheduled, gated and approved.

Only steps 2, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 10 are Python jobs (plus step 1, which runs inside main.py); the three *-load steps are a single CALL <schema>.sp_load_all(...) inside PostgreSQL (main.py:run_load). A failing step stops the run unless --keep-going is passed.

Step 1 (preflight, src/utils/preflight.py) sends one cheap statement to each source - PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Databricks - with capped exponential backoff, so an unreachable source or a rejected Databricks token stops the run before Spark starts. Airflow keeps its own banking_airflow.preflight task (Java, disk, Maven, SMTP) and runs the other nine through main.py --only <step>.

docs.title: Extracts in detail (step 2)
docs.text:
The three extractors share src/utils/extract_runner.py. Each table follows the same safe, twice-runnable loop (src/utils/spark_io.py):

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant X as extract_<source>.py
    participant A as audit
    participant S as source system
    participant P as PostgreSQL

    X->>A: fail_stale_runs(6h) · start_pipeline_run
    loop each enabled table
        X->>A: table_run(...) opens RUNNING row
        alt incremental
            X->>A: get_watermark + begin_batch (lock_version)
            X->>S: MAX(incremental_column)
            Note over X: skip when there is no new data
        end
        X->>S: Spark reads ONLY the batch window
        X->>P: write raw._stg_<table>
        X->>P: ONE transaction: promote → raw + advance_watermark
        X->>P: drop raw._stg_<table>
        X->>A: row_count_source_vs_landed
        X->>A: close table_run (SUCCESS/FAILED/SKIPPED)
    end
    X->>A: finish_pipeline_run (SUCCESS/PARTIAL/FAILED)

Key points:

  • Snapshot, read, promote, advance. The window is [last_watermark, MAX(source col)]. Spark writes to a transient raw._stg_<table>, then one Postgres transaction promotes it to raw.<table> and advances the watermark. If anything fails before that commit, the target and watermark are untouched, so a retry simply re-extracts the same window.
  • Upper bound re-reads the boundary. MySQL/Mongo use >= on the lower bound (dedupe happens in staging); Databricks uses strict > because created_at is often shared by a whole batch (spark_io._dbx_where).
  • Schemaless sources are tamed. Mongo dates/ids arrive as strings; cast_temporal, cast_integers, and prepare_for_jdbc convert them (structs/maps → jsonb). MySQL columns get exact Postgres types from information_schema. Databricks results are streamed through Arrow to local Parquet (memory-flat, no JDBC driver).
  • Schema drift is absorbed. promote_staging creates the target on first run and adds new source columns automatically (ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN).

docs.text:
Two separate watermark stores. They must never be conflated (docs/AUDIT.md).

        SRC[("source")] -->|Spark read window| RAW[("raw.<table>")]
        RAW -.->|advance in same txn| EW[("audit.extract_watermarks")]
        EW -.->|next window start| SRC
    end
    subgraph STG["staging · raw → staging"]
        RAW2[("raw.<table>")] -->|"sp_load filters > wm"| STG2[("staging.<table>")]
        STG2 -.->|advance in same block| TW[("audit.etl_watermarks")]
        TW -.->|next window start| RAW2
    end

    classDef raw fill:#ffedd5,stroke:#c2410c,color:#7c2d12,stroke-width:2px

  • audit.extract_watermarks — last source value landed into raw, advanced by advance_watermark inside the extract transaction; bootstrapped by scripts/seed_watermarks.py.
  • audit.etl_watermarks — last raw value consumed into staging, advanced by each staging.sp_load_* (defaults to _loaded_at).
  • Both use optimistic locking (lock_version): begin_batch snapshots it, advance_watermark updates WHERE lock_version = expected and raises a conflict (→ rollback) if a concurrent run won.
  • Full loads (MySQL) have no watermark and TRUNCATE + INSERT atomically, so readers never see an empty table.

  1. Watermarks advance only inside the load/extract transaction; extract_watermarks (source→raw) and etl_watermarks (raw→staging) are never mixed.

  3. A critical DQ failure blocks publish.
  4. raw, staging, analytics, marts are written only by their owners.
  5. Money is NUMERIC(18,2); all instants are timezone-aware UTC.
  6. Audit rows survive failure; the DQ gate commits before it raises.
  7. Never weaken, skip or delete a test, hook or CI check to get green — fix the code or ask.

docs.title: Rules that must not break
docs.text:
• Watermarks advance only inside the load/extract transaction; the two stores are never conflated.
  • Every load is safe to run twice with the same input.

docs.title: Data Contracts
docs.text:
A data contract is a checked-in JSON file that pins the shape of one table as it crosses a boundary. In this project the boundary is source → raw landing: a contract states what the source system is allowed to send, what the pipeline promises to store, and how the table is quality-checked. If the contract is valid, the pipeline has a right to assume the data conforms; if the source changes shape, the contract is what fails first — in CI, before the run.

Contracts live under contracts/, one file per table, validated by contracts/validate.py, and they are the machine-readable companion to audit.source_tables in sql/scripts/03_register_sources.sql.

contracts/
├── source-table.schema.json     # JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) — the contract of contracts
├── registry.json                # mirror of audit.source_tables (all 10 landing tables)
├── validate.py                  # validator used by pre-commit, make contracts and CI
├── __init__.py
├── mysql/
│   ├── accounts.json            # one file per landed table
│   └── customers.json
├── mongodb/
│   └── support_tickets.json
├── databricks/
│   └── transactions.json
└── example_table/               # worked template (skipped by registry check)
    └── example_table.json

There are two ways to read validity:

  • source-table.schema.json — the JSON Schema, for tooling and editors.
  • contracts/validate.py — the enforced judgements (naming, referential integrity against columns, money types, watermark rules), run in CI. The schema and the validator are kept in step; when they disagree, the validator wins because it is what the gate runs.

docs.title: File format
docs.text:
Every field is defined in source-table.schema.json. A full example:

{
  "contract_version": 1,
  "name": "accounts",
  "description": "MySQL account master. Full load; amounts are NUMERIC(18,2), never float.",
  "source": "mysql_source",
  "source_schema": "banking_core_db",
  "source_table": "accounts",
  "target_schema": "raw",
  "target_table": "accounts",
  "business_key": ["account_id"],
  "load_strategy": "full",
  "num_partitions": 4,
  "columns": [
    { "name": "account_id", "type": "bigint", "nullable": false, "key": true },
    { "name": "balance", "type": "numeric(18,2)", "nullable": true }
  ],
  "quality": {
    "row_count": { "mode": "source_vs_landed_exact", "severity": "ERROR" },
    "freshness": {
      "mode": "max_loaded_at_within_window",
      "window": "PT24H",
      "compare": "landing_loaded_at",
      "severity": "WARNING"
    }
  },
  "owner": "banking-data-platform",
  "tags": ["master-data"]
}

docs.title: Field reference
docs.text: Field Required Rules contract_version yes must be 1. Bump only with a migration of every contract. name yes snake_case; equals target_table; equals the file name. description yes ≥ 8 chars; say what the table is and where it comes from. source yes one of mongodb_source, mysql_source, databricks_source. source_schema yes e.g. banking_core_db, banking_support_db, public. source_table yes name in the source system. target_schema yes must be raw for a landing contract. target_table yes snake_case; matches the file name and registry.json. business_key yes non-empty list of column names that must exist in columns. load_strategy yes full or incremental. incremental_column if incremental snake_case (leading _ allowed, e.g. _id). Null/absent for full loads. watermark_strategy if incremental timestamp, numeric or objectid. Null/absent for full loads. match_mode no strict_gt (default) or inclusive_gte; how the watermark filter compares. lookback no ISO-8601 duration (PT6H) re-read to absorb late arrivals. num_partitions no integer ≥ 1; read parallelism hint (mirrors source_tables). columns[] yes non-empty, unique name, no duplicates, each type from the allowed set. columns[].type yes see the table below. Money is numeric(18,2), never float. columns[].nullable no true only if the source can genuinely emit null. columns[].key no mark business-key columns; must be consistent with business_key. columns[].pii no true for names, DOB, phone, email; drives masking in marts. quality.row_count.mode yes source_vs_landed_exact or source_vs_landed_tolerant. quality.row_count.tolerance_ratio if tolerant 0–1. quality.row_count.severity yes ERROR blocks publish; WARNING only reports. quality.freshness.mode yes max_loaded_at_within_window or none. quality.freshness.window if not none ISO-8601 duration, e.g. PT24H. quality.freshness.compare no landing_loaded_at (default) or source_incremental_column. quality.freshness.severity yes ERROR or WARNING. owner no team or GitHub handle responsible for the contract. tags no free-form labels (master-data, pii, incremental, …).

docs.title: Allowed column types
docs.text:
Landing types are deliberately Postgres-shaped. Anything else is rejected.

bigint  integer  smallint
numeric(18,2)  numeric(5,2)          -- money / rates; never float
double precision                     -- measurements only, never money
boolean  text  date  timestamptz  jsonb
  • timestamptz for every instant. Sources are UTC; naive datetimes are a bug.
  • numeric(18,2) for money. A CI test fails any amount/balance/income column that is not numeric(18,2).
  • MongoDB dates arrive as strings and are cast during landing, so the contract still declares the landed type (timestamptz).

docs.title: Landed audit columns
docs.text: Do not declare _batch_id or _loaded_at. Every landing write adds them (src/utils/spark_io.py:add_audit_columns): _batch_id is the table_run_id (a UUID) that produced the row and _loaded_at is the write timestamp. Both are owned by the pipeline, so a contract that lists them fails validation.

docs.title: Watermarks and idempotency
docs.text:
Contracts are what make a load safe to run twice:

  • incremental_column + watermark_strategy describe the high-water mark. The watermark is advanced only inside the same transaction as the write, so a crash leaves the watermark where the data is. Never mix audit.extract_watermarks (MySQL/Mongo) with audit.etl_watermarks.
  • match_mode: strict_gt reads strictly newer than the mark (the default). inclusive_gte re-reads the boundary row; use lookback with it to absorb late-arriving rows. The write is idempotent, so re-reads are safe.
  • objectid strategy orders MongoDB documents by _id; created_at in those collections is a plain string and cannot be a timestamp watermark.
  • full loads redefine the table every run; their contract must leave incremental_column and watermark_strategy empty.

docs.title: The registry mirror
docs.text: contracts/registry.json is a machine-readable copy of audit.source_tables (all 10 landing tables). A test asserts that for every contract the registry agrees on source, business_key, load_strategy, incremental_column and watermark_strategy. SQL is the source of truth: when you register or change a table, edit 03_register_sources.sql first, then registry.json and the contract in the same PR.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
Run it three ways; all of them execute the same code.

make contracts                                  # all files
uv run python -m contracts.validate             # same thing
uv run python -m contracts.validate contracts/mysql/accounts.json

contracts/validate.py fails with a path-prefixed reason, e.g.:

contract validation failed:
  - contracts/mysql/accounts.json: business_key column 'account' is not in columns

The gate runs in:

  • pre-commit — staged contracts/**/*.json must parse and validate.
  • pre-push — every contracts/**/*.json must parse.
  • CI (make contracts, Linux and Windows) and make ci locally.
  • tests/unit/test_contracts.py — discovery, per-file validity, name/type rules, registry agreement and negative cases.

docs.title: Adding a contract
docs.text:
1. Register the table in sql/scripts/03_register_sources.sql (idempotent) and apply it to the warehouse.
  2. Copy contracts/example_table/example_table.json to contracts/<source>/<target_table>.json and fill in the fields.
  3. Add the row to contracts/registry.json to match the SQL.
  4. Run make contracts until clean, then make ci.
  5. Commit SQL, registry and contract together; the PR template reminds you.

docs.title: Changing or removing a contract
docs.text:
• Non-breaking (add a nullable column, add an optional field): one PR.
  • Breaking (rename/retype/drop a column, change a business key or watermark): additive-then-migrate. Land the new column, backfill, switch readers, then remove the old column in a later PR. Never edit a merged contract to match a silent source change — treat it as an incident.
  • Removing a table: remove it from the SQL registry, registry.json, the contract file and its tests in the same PR.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• JSON only, no comments; snake_case names.
  • name, target_table and the file name always agree.
  • Money is numeric(18,2); instants are timestamptz; never float.
  • Landing audit columns are pipeline-owned; do not declare them.
  • SQL registry is the source of truth; the mirror and contracts follow it.
  • The validator is part of the gate. Do not weaken it to make a red build green.

docs.title: Data quality — Banking-Delta-Lakehouse
docs.text: Every layer is gated by a SQL data-quality suite that runs against the warehouse before the next layer may load. A critical failure blocks publish. This is data testing; code testing lives in docs/TESTING.md.

docs.title: Gate flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    DISC["discover *.sql<br/>numeric order"] --> APPLY["CREATE OR REPLACE<br/>audit.dq_<layer>_<check>"]
    APPLY --> CALL["CALL each procedure"]
    CALL --> RUN[("audit.dq_run")]
    CALL --> VIO[("audit.dq_violation")]
    CALL --> LAT[("audit.v_dq_latest")]
    RUN --> VERDICT{"any FAIL?"}
    VIO --> VERDICT
    VERDICT -->|no| PASS["exit 0: gate open"]
    VERDICT -->|yes| FAIL["raise + exit 1: gate blocks publish"]

    classDef step fill:#e0e7ff,stroke:#4338ca,color:#312e81,stroke-width:2px
    classDef audit fill:#f1f5f9,stroke:#475569,color:#1e293b,stroke-width:2px
    classDef ok fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#15803d,color:#14532d,stroke-width:2px
    classDef bad fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#b91c1c,color:#7f1d1d,stroke-width:2px

Colour: indigo = runner steps, slate = audit tables, green = pass, red = fail.

The non-zero exit is the gate that blocks publish in Airflow and main.py.

docs.title: Suite layout
docs.text:
tests/data-quality/
├── raw/        10 tests + 00_master_raw_tests.sql
├── staging/    10 tests + 00_master_staging_tests.sql
├── analytics/  13 tests + 00_master_analytics_tests.sql
│               + 00_lp_check_upstream_freshness.sql (helper function)
└── marts/      11 tests + 00_master_marts_tests.sql

Runners: scripts/run_{raw,staging,analytics,marts}_tests.py (discover in numeric order, Rich progress, exit non-zero on any failure). Make targets: make dq-raw … make dq-marts, or make dq for all four in layer order. Airflow runs the same runners as *_tests steps of banking_delta_daily.

python scripts/run_staging_tests.py --list     # what would run
python scripts/run_staging_tests.py --only 03  # one check
python scripts/run_staging_tests.py --master   # the layer's master procedure

docs.title: The per-file contract
docs.text:
Each file NN_<check>.sql defines one procedure audit.dq_<layer>_<check>() that:

  1. inserts an audit.dq_run row (layer, script_name);
  2. inserts one audit.dq_violation per bad row/message;
  3. updates the run with violation_count and PASS/FAIL;
  4. COMMITs, then RAISEs on failure — the one place COMMIT is allowed inside SQL on purpose, so the audit reason survives the rollback.

The smoke suite (tests/smoke/test_sql_contract.py) enforces this: master file present, unique numeric prefixes (excluding 00/99), procedure named audit.dq_*, dq_run + dq_violation written, procedure called by 00_master_<layer>_tests.sql, and COMMIT-before-RAISE (comment lines ignored).

A 00_* file other than the master is a DDL-only helper: it defines a function other checks CALL (e.g. analytics/00_lp_check_upstream_freshness.sql → audit.dq_analytics_upstream_lag()), declares no procedure and writes no audit rows, so it is excluded from the contract above and never CALLed. Because the runner applies files it discovers, a full run creates it before 01 needs it — running --only 01 on its own uses whatever version is already in the database (re-apply it with --only 00).

docs.title: Check catalogue
docs.text: # Check What it proves 01 metadata_col _batch_id / _loaded_at present, NOT NULL, timestamptz, not future, and not more than 1 h behind the staging table it is built from (30 days of silence warns, never fails) 02 primary_keys PK/unique columns are non-null and unique 03 bad_dates no NULL/impossible/future dates 04 orphan_rows every FK has a parent row (e.g. accounts → customers) 05 business_rules amounts ≥ 0, valid statuses, plausible rates 06 numeric_ranges numeric columns inside agreed min/max bands 07 schema_contract columns and types match the expected contract 08 completeness no unexpected NULLs / coverage thresholds met 09 duplicate_rows no duplicate business keys or whole-row duplicates 10 value_domains categorical values inside the allowed domain 11 date_key_integrity (analytics) date keys resolve to the dim date 12 derived_attributes (analytics) derived bands/attributes are consistent 13 reconciliation (analytics + marts) fact totals reconcile with their sources

docs.title: Adding or changing a check
docs.text:
1. File: tests/data-quality/<layer>/NN_<check>.sql — next free number; the runner discovers in numeric order.
  2. One CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE audit.dq_<layer>_<check>() following the contract above. Style: uppercase keywords, snake_case, explicit column lists (make sql-lint).
  3. Exclude transient landing tables in raw-layer schema checks: c.relname NOT LIKE '\_stg\_%'.
  4. Register it in 00_master_<layer>_tests.sql.
  5. Validate: make sql-lint (always) → python scripts/run_<layer>_tests.py --only NN -v against a disposable or approved DB (ask first).
  6. Prove it can fail: insert one bad row on a disposable DB, confirm exit code ≠ 0, then remove it. A check that cannot fail is worthless.
  7. Never relax a threshold to make a layer pass — investigate the data or ask.

docs.title: Rules that must not break
docs.text:
• A critical DQ failure blocks publish.
  • Audit rows are committed before the failure is raised.
  • Landing tables _stg_% are transient and excluded from schema checks.
  • The suites are data tests: they need a populated warehouse, so they are never part of make ci and never run against production without approval.

docs.title: Architecture decision log — Banking-Delta-Lakehouse
docs.text:
Why the pipeline is built the way it is. Each entry derives from ARCHITECTURE.md, docs/, the code and commit messages. Where no rationale is documented, the entry describes what the code actually does.

# Decision Status 1 PostgreSQL stored procedures for transformation, not dbt accepted 2 Four PostgreSQL layers (raw → staging → analytics → marts) accepted 3 PySpark used for extraction only accepted 4 Watermark/incremental strategy; late-arriving data handling accepted 5 Airflow for orchestration, no logic in the DAGs accepted 6 Data-quality gates at every layer accepted 7 Publish marts to Databricks Delta accepted 8 Read-only Streamlit consumer accepted 9 Data contracts at the source → raw landing boundary accepted

docs.title: 1. PostgreSQL stored procedures for transformation, not dbt
docs.text:
Decision: Every transform from raw through marts is a plpgsql stored procedure (staging.sp_load_*, analytics.sp_load_dim|fact_*, marts.sp_load_mart_*, masters sp_load_all), deployed with psql -f and invoked as one CALL <schema>.sp_load_all(...) per layer (main.py:run_load).

Alternatives rejected: dbt (generated SQL, warehouse-agnostic, lineage and test ecosystem); Python/PySpark transforms against the warehouse; plain versioned SQL scripts without procedures.

Why: Procedures keep each load in a single transaction with the advisory lock, OUT row counts and the watermark advance (AGENTS.md SQL standards; ARCHITECTURE.md §6). The watermark-advance-in-transaction invariant (ARCHITECTURE.md §2.4) is therefore enforced by the procedure that performs the write, so a crash leaves both the data and the watermark untouched and a retry re-reads the same window. Idempotency is built from the same transaction boundary: loads are safe to run twice, and full loads TRUNCATE + INSERT atomically (ARCHITECTURE.md §6). Commits de3e289 (analytics procedures), 98157e5 (mart procedures), 4c5bcba (deploy via psql) show the layer-by-layer adoption. No dbt configuration exists anywhere in the repo. This explains why procedures meet the invariants; the repo does not record a separate evaluation of dbt.

Trade-offs / at larger scale: Procedures couple the transforms to PostgreSQL and their lineage is weaker than dbt's graph. I would keep the transactional invariants but add dbt (or pg_stat_statements-driven docs) on top for lineage, documentation and modular tests once more than one engineer edits the transforms.

docs.title: 2. Four PostgreSQL layers (raw → staging → analytics → marts)
docs.text:
Decision: Landing (raw, as-is + _batch_id/_loaded_at), cleansing (staging, typed/deduped SCD1), modelling (analytics, dim_*/fact_* star schema) and serving (marts, business-shaped mart_*), each written only by its owner and each gated before the next loads (ARCHITECTURE.md §5, §14.4).

Alternatives rejected: three layers (fold cleansing into landing); a single schema with views; loading source systems straight into marts.

Why: Separation lets the DQ suite test a different contract per layer — schema at landing, types and keys at staging, grain and orphans at analytics, business rules at marts (docs/DATA-QUALITY.md). Raw stays replayable: any layer can be rebuilt from raw without touching the sources. Layer ownership is a written invariant (ARCHITECTURE.md §14.4), enforced by having exactly one owner per schema.

Trade-offs / at larger scale: Four layers duplicate storage and add a full load cycle per hop. I would keep the contract boundaries but partition raw by _loaded_at and add TTL on staging._stg_* artefacts as volume grows; merging staging into raw would only be reconsidered if landing became typed.

docs.title: 3. PySpark used for extraction only
docs.text:
Decision: Spark appears only in step 2 (run_jobs.py → extract_*.py → src/utils/spark_io.py) to read the three sources and write raw._stg_<table>. All transformation is SQL inside PostgreSQL.

Alternatives rejected: Spark/Delta for the whole pipeline (Spark SQL warehouse); plain Python connectors (pymysql/pymongo) for extraction with no Spark; ETL logic inside the extract jobs.

Why: The sources need what Spark gives — the Mongo connector, JDBC with exact Postgres types, partitioning hints, and streaming Databricks results through Arrow to local Parquet (ARCHITECTURE.md §4). Transformations run where the watermarks and transactions live, so the extract layer never decides business logic. src/utils/engine.py exists only to tune and pre-flight-check that one Spark session.

Trade-offs / at larger scale: Two engines (Spark + Postgres) to operate and tune. I would keep Spark for extraction but move heavy transforms to a Spark/Delta layer only if Postgres transform time became the bottleneck — today a full run is ~9 min (README metrics), so it is not.

docs.title: 4. Watermark/incremental strategy; late-arriving data
docs.text:
Decision: Two separate stores — audit.extract_watermarks (source → raw, advanced by advance_watermark inside the extract transaction) and audit.etl_watermarks (raw → staging, advanced by each staging.sp_load_*). Both use optimistic lock_version; the window is [last_watermark, MAX(source col)] with the lower bound inclusive on MySQL/Mongo and strict > on Databricks (spark_io._dbx_where). Full loads (MySQL) are atomic TRUNCATE + INSERT.

Alternatives rejected: one shared watermark table; advancing watermarks after the commit (outside the transaction); full refresh of every table each run; event-time watermarks à la Flink.

Why: Advancing the mark in the same transaction as the write means a crash neither loses nor double-counts rows (ARCHITECTURE.md §2.4, §6), and the two stores are never conflated (§14.1). Late arrivals are absorbed by the inclusive boundary re-read plus an optional lookback duration per contract (docs/CONTRACTS.md: "inclusive_gte re-reads the boundary row; use lookback with it to absorb late-arriving rows. The write is idempotent, so re-reads are safe"), and at publish time by re-reading the last N months (--lookback / PUBLISH_LOOKBACK_MONTHS, ARCHITECTURE.md §9).

Trade-offs / at larger scale: The inclusive bound re-reads the boundary row every run (safe because writes are idempotent, but wasted work at volume). The known gap is that PUBLISH_LOOKBACK_MONTHS=0 (default) does not republish old months — it caused the mart_support_performance 193-row gap (docs/RUNBOOK.md); a durable non-zero lookback or periodic --full is an open item. I would default lookback on and add a nightly reconciliation of source vs published counts (the publish_reconcile report already visualises it, docs/REPORTING.md).

docs.title: 5. Airflow for orchestration, no logic in the DAGs
docs.text:
Decision: Airflow 3.3.2 (CeleryExecutor, Docker Compose) schedules three DAGs; every task shells out to the same scripts main.py runs (airflow/dags/banking_delta_daily.py → main.py → run_jobs.py). The DAGs hold wiring, retries, pools and alerting only (ARCHITECTURE.md §2.1, §10).

Alternatives rejected: cron + shell scripts; Prefect/Dagster; putting pipeline logic directly in DAG tasks; running only by hand via main.py.

Why: "One way to run the pipeline" — Airflow adds scheduling, retries, pools and alerting without ever diverging from the manual path (ARCHITECTURE.md §2.1). The design earns its keep operationally: preflight fails in seconds on missing Java/disk/warehouse, DQ-gate tasks use retries=0 because a data problem does not fix itself, banking_watchdog reads audit.pipeline_runs and stays silent when healthy (§10). Commits a99af09 (Airflow/deployment/runbook guides) and bfc6e32 (decide_status fails closed) document the operational hardening.

Trade-offs / at larger scale: A Celery + Redis + Postgres stack is heavy for a single maintainer. I would keep Airflow (it is already logic-free and testable) but move to a managed/remote executor and split the spark_jvm pool weights per source as concurrency grows; the watchdog and all_done finalisers would stay.

docs.title: 6. Data-quality gates at every layer
docs.text:
Decision: Each layer has a SQL suite under tests/data-quality/{layer}/ whose files define audit.dq_<layer>_<check>() procedures; they write audit.dq_run + audit.dq_violation, COMMIT the verdict before RAISE, and the runner's non-zero exit blocks the next layer and publish (ARCHITECTURE.md §8).

Alternatives rejected: Great Expectations — explicitly not used (CLAUDE.md: "Validation: SQL DQ suites, not Great Expectations"); CI-only tests that never look at the loaded data; spot-check/sampling gates; Python assertions after the load.

Why: The gate tests the data in the warehouse, not the code — a contract drift or upstream hole must stop publish before a consumer sees it (docs/DATA-QUALITY.md). Commit-before-raise is the one intentional COMMIT in SQL so the failure reason survives the rollback (ARCHITECTURE.md §8). The check catalogue (metadata, keys, dates, orphans, ranges, schema, completeness, duplicates, domains, reconciliation) is enforced per file, and tests/smoke/test_sql_contract.py pins the per-file contract in CI.

Trade-offs / at larger scale: SQL checks are tied to the Postgres dialect and their catalogue is hand-maintained. I would keep them as the gate but add cross-system reconciliation (source vs raw vs Delta row counts per key) as a fifth suite, and generate the check list from the contracts so a new contract column cannot ship without a check.

docs.title: 7. Publish marts to Databricks Delta
docs.text:
Decision: Step 10 (src/jobs/publish_marts.py) reads PostgreSQL marts.mart_* windowed by the watermark read from the Delta target itself, writes local Parquet via pyarrow, uploads to a Unity Catalog volume and runs one MERGE INTO … USING read_files(...) (keyed marts) or INSERT OVERWRITE (snapshots) (ARCHITECTURE.md §9).

Alternatives rejected: row-by-row JDBC inserts into Delta; external tables/federation reading Postgres directly from Databricks; replicating with Debezium/CDC; making the dashboard query PostgreSQL.

Why: The dashboard consumes Databricks SQL, so marts must exist there; reading the watermark from the target makes publish self-incrementing with no extra state (ARCHITECTURE.md §9). Parquet + read_files avoids a JDBC driver inside Databricks and keeps the whole publish idempotent (MERGE on keys).

Trade-offs / at larger scale: The documented gap is the publish lookback: with PUBLISH_LOOKBACK_MONTHS=0 late/edited rows in older months are not republished (docs/RUNBOOK.md, the 193-row mart_support_performance gap; docs/REPORTING.md says publish_reconcile exists because of it). I would turn a non-zero lookback on by default, add a nightly source-vs-Delta count gate, and consider Delta Sharing if consumers multiply.

docs.title: 8. Read-only Streamlit consumer
docs.text:
Decision: The Streamlit dashboard (dashboard/) only SELECTs from published Databricks Delta marts and never writes to any layer (dashboard/README.md, ARCHITECTURE.md colour legend: indigo = read-only consumers).

Alternatives rejected: consumers writing results back into the warehouse; dashboards querying PostgreSQL directly; a serving API with write endpoints; giving consumers service accounts with DDL rights.

Why: Consumers sit behind the publish boundary, so a bad query cannot corrupt the warehouse — layer ownership (ARCHITECTURE.md §14.4) stays intact. The dashboard caches each SELECT for 5 minutes to protect the SQL warehouse (dashboard/README.md). The report collector is guarded by a test that issues only SELECT statements (docs/TESTING.md).

Trade-offs / at larger scale: Read-only means every new derived figure must first be modelled into a mart (slow for ad-hoc work). I would keep the rule for anything shared, and add a sandbox schema/consumer with quotas for exploration instead of relaxing the marts' read-only contract.

docs.title: 9. Data contracts at the source → raw landing boundary
docs.text:
Decision: One JSON contract per source table under contracts/, a registry.json mirroring audit.source_tables, a JSON Schema (source-table.schema.json) and contracts/validate.py run by make contracts, the pre-commit hook and CI — the contract pins what a source may send before any row lands (docs/CONTRACTS.md).

Alternatives rejected: contracts at every layer boundary; no contracts (schema-on-read); contracts expressed only as database migrations; contracts derived at runtime from information_schema.

Why: "If the source changes shape, the contract is what fails first — in CI, before the run" (docs/CONTRACTS.md). It is the machine-readable companion to audit.source_tables, so extract config and schema expectations cannot drift apart. Commit 850b790 (feat(contracts): add validated source landing contracts) introduced the schema, registry and validator together with the CI gate.

Trade-offs / at larger scale: Contracts cover only the landing boundary; staging and mart schemas are guarded by DQ schema_contract checks instead of contracts proper. I would extend the same JSON-Schema approach to each layer's output (staging, analytics, marts) so every hop has a checked-in expectation, once the mart schemas stabilise.

docs.title: Deployment — Banking-Delta-Lakehouse
docs.text:
Four pieces deploy independently: the local toolchain, the PostgreSQL warehouse, the Airflow stack (Docker Compose) and the Streamlit dashboard. Databricks is consumed, not deployed. Nothing here runs without real credentials — see AGENTS.md permissions first.

Colour legend: docs/PIPELINE.md.

docs.title: 1. Local toolchain
docs.text:
make install        # uv sync --group dev (Python >= 3.13 pinned in pyproject.toml)
make hooks          # git config core.hooksPath .githooks — mandatory
make ci             # gate: lint + sql-lint + unit + smoke + report-fixture

Prerequisites: uv, GNU Make (Windows: choco make, or tasks.bat <target> without Make), Java 8/11/17/21 for Spark paths, git. Copy .env.example → .env and fill real values — .env is git-ignored and must never be committed.

make report-pdf needs a TeX distribution with latexmk and pdflatex (TinyTeX or TeX Live are enough). Without TeX, make report-fixture still renders the documents and make report-docker builds the PDF inside the container instead.

docs.title: 2. PostgreSQL warehouse
docs.text:
Bootstrap is ordered, idempotent SQL under sql/scripts/ (apply in numeric order, excluding 00_create_database if the DB already exists, and 05_switch_* once the flip is done):

# Script Purpose 00 00_create_database.sql create banking_delta 01 01_init_schemas.sql raw, staging, analytics, marts, audit (+ exploration) 02 02_audit_tables.sql registry, runs, errors, etl_watermarks, table_runs 03 03_register_sources.sql seed 3 sources + 10 tables (Mongo/Databricks incremental, MySQL full) 04 04_dq_audit_tables.sql dq_run, dq_violation, v_dq_latest 05 05_switch_mongo_databricks_incremental.sql one-time full → incremental flip (03 cannot update existing rows) 06 06_extract_watermarks.sql extract_watermarks (separate from etl_watermarks)

Then the layer procedures and DQ suites:

make sql-smoke                 # disposable DB only: sql/** + tests/data-quality/** (ALLOW_SQL_SMOKE=1)
python scripts/seed_watermarks.py   # FIRST incremental run of a new table (never for MySQL)

Procedure layers: sql/{staging,analytics,marts}/NN_*.sql + 00_master_load.sql, applied in numeric order (parent → child). Merged migrations are never edited — add a new numbered file (AGENTS.md).

docs.title: 3. Airflow stack
docs.text:
Full detail: docs/AIRFLOW.md. Short version:

cd airflow
cp .env.airflow.example .env.airflow                    # real secrets per environment
# .env.airflow also holds AIRFLOW_VERSION (passed via --env-file for compose interpolation)
docker compose --env-file .env.airflow up airflow-init  # must exit 0
docker compose --env-file .env.airflow up -d
# local dev from the repo root instead: make up / make down
#   (adds docker-compose.dev.yml bind mounts and exports GIT_SHA from git)
# UI: http://127.0.0.1:8080 — un-pause banking_delta_daily and banking_report_weekly deliberately
  • Image bakes the project venv + code + TeX toolchain (airflow/Dockerfile reads reports/apt-packages.txt); docker-compose.dev.yml bind-mounts the repo for development.
  • Environment per stage = .env.airflow content (PG_*, MYSQL_*, MONGO_*, DATABRICKS_*, SMTP_*, REPORT_*). Keep it out of git.
  • Compose passes ENVIRONMENT (defaults to development) and GIT_SHA into every container. Set ENVIRONMENT explicitly for staging/production — the default would otherwise label a non-development run as development in the mail and the PDF.
  • The worker needs the spark_cache volume (Ivy jars), the report_output volume (PDF artefacts for mail attachment) and ~6 GB.

docs.title: 4. Dashboard
docs.text:
cd dashboard
python -m venv .venv && .venv\Scripts\activate     # or source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .streamlit/secrets.toml.example .streamlit/secrets.toml   # fill real values
streamlit run app.py                               # http://localhost:8501

Docker: docker build -t banking-dashboard . → docker run -p 8501:8501 banking-dashboard (secrets as env vars or a mounted secrets file). .streamlit/secrets.toml is git-ignored. The app is read-only and shows only published Databricks marts.

docs.title: 5. GitHub Pages (documentation site)
docs.text:
The docs/ tree (plus root ARCHITECTURE.md, included at build time via docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) is built with MkDocs Material and published from the gh-pages branch by .github/workflows/pages.yml:

URL Source Notes https://nitinx12.github.io/Banking-Delta-Lakehouse/ main production site root https://nitinx12.github.io/Banking-Delta-Lakehouse/preview/dev/ dev noindex https://nitinx12.github.io/Banking-Delta-Lakehouse/preview/staging/ staging noindex https://nitinx12.github.io/Banking-Delta-Lakehouse/preview/qa/ qa noindex
  • Every push to main/dev/staging/qa runs uv sync --group docs + uv run mkdocs build --strict and publishes with keep_files, so previews and production coexist on one gh-pages branch (shared concurrency group, no cancel-in-progress). Preview builds set MKDOCS_NOINDEX=true.
  • No site_url is configured: all links are relative, which is what makes the same build work at / and /preview/<branch>/.
  • Local preview: uv sync --group docs && uv run mkdocs build --strict (output in site_build/, git-ignored — site/ holds the landing-page helpers; copy assets/ into site_build/assets/ if you want the insight charts to render).

Promotion flow: dev → staging → qa → main, one merge per hop; each merge republishes that branch's preview immediately, and the merge into main promotes it to the production root.

Rollback: revert the offending commit on main (or the branch) and push — the site is republished from the pushed commit (the production root is overwritten in place; keep_files preserves the preview directories between deploys). Preview branches roll back the same way. One-time setup: Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch → gh-pages / / (root).

docs.title: Secrets rules
docs.text:
• Never commit .env, airflow/.env.airflow, .streamlit/secrets.toml, tokens or keys.
  • Pre-commit blocks secret-like filenames; mail/audit redaction (redact.py, src.utils.audit._redact) is defense-in-depth, not a licence to log secrets.
  • Production credentials never reach CI (AGENTS.md; .gitleaks.toml + make leaks are still to be added).

docs.title: Promotion checklist
docs.text:
• make ci green (lint + contracts + sql-lint + unit + smoke)
  • new migrations added as numbered files, applied twice to confirm idempotence
  • .env.example updated for new variables; smoke tests updated
  • docs/ updated if behaviour or targets changed
  • restricted actions (warehouse runs, merges) approved per AGENTS.md

docs.title: CI/CD and Git workflow — Banking-Delta-Lakehouse
docs.text: How a change travels from a branch to production. CI runs the same make targets you run locally (tasks.bat on Windows), so green locally means green in CI. Workflows live in .github/workflows/. Rules for AI agents (AGENTS.md) always win on conflict.

docs.title: Ground rules
docs.text:
1. One concern per branch, one logical change per commit, small diffs. Branches live days, not weeks.
  2. Conventional Commits, hooks always on. --no-verify is forbidden.
  3. Never commit .env, tokens, *.pem, *.key, id_rsa, file.txt.
  4. Never force-push. Never edit an already-merged SQL migration; add a new numbered file.
  5. Never weaken, skip or delete a test to get CI green. Tests ship with the behaviour they cover; a bug fix includes a regression test that fails first.

docs.title: Branches and setup
docs.text:
Prefix Use Example feature/ new capability feature/publish-lookback-config fix/ bug fix fix/summary-task-states chore/ tooling, deps, config, test scaffolding chore/test-scaffold docs/ documentation only docs/project-docs test/ tests only (use chore/ if disallowed) test/audit-redact-unit

Lowercase kebab-case, always from an up-to-date main (git pull --ff-only). One-time setup per clone:

make install   # uv sync --group dev
make hooks     # git config core.hooksPath .githooks (mandatory; verify it prints .githooks)

Hooks (.githooks/): commit-msg enforces Conventional Commits; pre-commit blocks secrets and key files and runs ruff check + ruff format --check on staged Python; pre-push runs a fast gate. If a hook fails, fix the cause. .pre-commit-config.yaml (optional) adds sqlfluff and hygiene checks.

docs.title: Commits
docs.text:
Format type(scope): imperative summary, at most 72 chars, no trailing period; the body explains why.

  • Types: feat fix refactor perf test docs chore build ci style revert
  • Scopes: extract audit spark-io engine publish main airflow dags sql staging analytics marts dq dashboard make batch hooks deps tests repo reports

Stage explicitly (git add <paths>, never blind -A) and review with git diff --staged. Never commit scratch dirs (.spark/ logs/ airflow/logs/ .venv/ .coverage htmlcov/ __pycache__/).

docs.title: The change loop
docs.text:
1  Read AGENTS.md and the relevant docs/ page; sync main; create branch
 2  Write or adjust the test FIRST (red, see docs/TESTING.md)
 3  Implement the smallest change (green)
 4  Narrow test:  uv run pytest path/to/test_x.py -q
 5  Fast gate:    make unit smoke        Full gate: make ci (lint + sql-lint + unit + smoke)
 6  Extra tiers the change needs (DB/Spark/live: ask first)
 7  Update docs and Makefile together if targets changed
 8  git add <paths>; git commit          (hooks must pass)
 9  git fetch origin; git merge origin/main; re-run make ci
10  git push -u origin <branch>; open PR; STOP. Do not merge.

Keep a branch current by merging origin/main; rebasing needs a force-push, which is forbidden. If history is messy, ask a human.

Pull requests: title is the Conventional Commit summary; aim for one concern under ~400 changed lines. Body: what and why, how tested (commands and real results), risk, rollback, and any approval used. Agents open the PR and stop; merging or pushing to main needs a human.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: Action Allowed Ask first Never Read; make lint / sql-lint / unit / cov / smoke / test / ci; code, tests, docs on a branch; commit; push your own branch; open PR yes make spark-smoke / sql-smoke / integration / smoke-live, make daily, python main.py, Airflow trigger yes Merge or push to main, tag, release, manual cd dispatch yes Commit secrets, write to Databricks public, edit a merged migration, force-push, test against production never

docs.title: SQL changes and invariants
docs.text:
• Changes to an existing database go in a new numbered file (sql/scripts/NN_<what>.sql), idempotent, applied in order; never edit 00–06 once merged. Procedure files (sql/{staging,analytics,marts}/NN_*.sql) are CREATE OR REPLACE; keep 00_master_load.sql order parent → child.
  • Run make sql-lint, and make sql-smoke (disposable PG, ALLOW_SQL_SMOKE=1, ask first) when procedures change. New or changed DQ checks go in docs/DATA-QUALITY.md.
  • Must not break: watermarks advance only inside the load/extract transaction (audit.extract_watermarks vs audit.etl_watermarks, never mixed, see docs/AUDIT.md); every load is idempotent; a critical DQ failure blocks publish; each layer is written only by its owner.

docs.title: ci jobs
docs.text:
Job What it checks workflow-lint actionlint + zizmor on .github (checksum-verified installs) gate uv lock --check, ruff, contracts, sqlfluff, smoke, unit + coverage gate, report fixture dep-audit pip-audit on the locked dependencies windows-gate The same checks via tasks.bat secrets-check Push to main only: are the source secrets configured? pipeline Full uv run main.py --keep-going on a GitHub-hosted runner with a disposable Postgres ci-success Aggregates every job above; the one required check for branch protection

pipeline runs only on push to main (never on PRs, so PR code never sees secrets) and is skipped while secrets are unset. Set the repo variable SKIP_MAIN_PY=true to skip it in an emergency. It runs after the merge, so it flags a broken main but cannot stop the merge. Superseded PR runs are cancelled; runs on main never are. The PR gate stays fast and external-free; tests/smoke/test_make_parity.py fails if a Makefile target is missing from tasks.bat or ci picks up a non-hermetic target. smoke-live and Airflow triggers never run in CI.

docs.title: Release and deploy
docs.text:
git tag v0.1.0 && git push origin v0.1.0   # on main, green ci; needs approval
  1. release checks the tag matches pyproject.toml, the commit is on main, and make ci passes, then creates the GitHub release (a tag with -, like v0.2.0-rc1, is a prerelease; re-runs are safe) and dispatches cd: prerelease → staging, stable → production.
  2. docker also fires on the tag and pushes sha-xxxxxxx, version (1.2.3, 1.2) and branch tags, with provenance and SBOM.
  3. cd runs one deploy at a time per environment:
  4. resolve: the commit must be on origin/main; production also needs a stable vX.Y.Z tag.
  5. gate: production only; re-runs lint, contracts, sql-lint, smoke and coverage.
  6. deploy: waits for a green docker run on the same commit (fails after 5 minutes if none exists), pulls the image, checks its revision label matches the commit, checks required secrets, and runs the container by digest with --keep-going.
  7. Production needs manual approval via GitHub Environment protection rules. A failed production deploy or gate opens an issue.

Manual deploy: run cd from the Actions tab with environment and ref (staging skips the gate). Rollback: run cd with production and the previous stable tag. This redeploys code only; it does not undo data side effects (watermarks, published marts), and a watermark reset needs owner approval (docs/DESIGN.md). There is no release: published trigger, because a hand-made release would deploy a tag that release never verified.

docs.title: Security rules
docs.text:
• Least-privilege permissions: everywhere (contents: read by default, widened per job).
  • No pull_request_target, so fork PRs never get secrets. Secrets reach only pipeline and cd.
  • Third-party actions are pinned by full commit SHA with a version comment; Dependabot bumps them. Copy SHAs from the releases page, since a wrong SHA fails with "unable to find version".
  • No caches in the release and cd paths; downloaded tools are checksum-verified. labeler keeps the dependencies label on Dependabot PRs by matching the dependabot/ branch.

docs.title: One-time setup (repo admin)
docs.text:
1. Branch protection on main: require a PR (1 approval, dismiss stale approvals), up-to-date branches, resolved conversations; block force pushes and deletions. Required checks: ci-success, gitleaks, analyze (python). Until then, nothing stops a direct push.
  2. Secrets: repository secrets for pipeline (MONGO_*, MYSQL_* incl. MYSQL_DB, DATABRICKS_* incl. HTTP_PATH, SCHEMA_PUBLIC). Environment secrets for cd: PG_*, DATABRICKS_*, PUBLISH_STAGE_VOLUME, MONGO_*, MYSQL_*. Point the pipeline's DATABRICKS_MARTS_SCHEMA at a CI-only schema if publish_marts writes there.
  3. Environments: create staging and production, require reviewers on production, and restrict both to main and v* tags.
  4. Code security: enable Dependabot alerts and security updates, and private vulnerability reporting (used by SECURITY.md). Replace placeholder handles in CODEOWNERS.

docs.text: Index of the business questions answered by the marts schema. Each finding links to a detail file with the exact query and chart.

docs.title: About the data
docs.text:
The underlying rows are CSV snapshots of the ten source tables (contracts/registry.json: 5 MySQL, 2 MongoDB, 3 Databricks public) shipped under data/raw/ and exported from the live sources by scripts/export_raw_csv.py; a clone loads them with make load-raw-csv. See the README's "About the data" section for the full description.

  • Origin: unverified. No generator or seed script exists anywhere in this repository or its git history, so the original source of the rows cannot be determined from the repo. TODO(owner): confirm whether the data was generated, taken from a public dataset, or is real.
  • Looks generated. The shipped CSVs show sequential integer keys, customerN@mailbank.com emails and branch names like Pune Branch 1 — patterns typical of generated data (observed in the files, not proof).
  • Not a benchmark. The fraud rate (0.499%), late-payment rate (12.01%) and value concentration (22.55% in the top 10% of customers) are properties of this dataset only, not real-world banking figures. Treat every finding below as a demonstration of analytical method on synthetic-looking data, not as a finding about any real bank.

docs.text:
Each result is reproducible with the linked SQL against banking_delta.

Domain Segment result So what SQL Customers Upper-Mid (36.12%) and High (32.88%) income bands hold 69.00% of transaction value from 32,786 of 47,640 active customers; average value is flat at 250,807-255,284 across every band. Target the value decile, not the income tier: average customer value barely moves by income, so income-based offers would over-serve low-value customers in high bands. customer_segments.sql Loans Late-payment rate is flat by loan size: 11.88% (<1L) to 12.04% (1-5L), a 0.16pp spread; loan types span 11.85-12.19%. Run reminders and collections across the whole book; there is no small-ticket or large-ticket segment to prioritise. loan_segments.sql Card fraud Fraud rate is 0.479% (Platinum) to 0.507% (Classic), a 0.028pp spread; Debit cards (tier N/A) carry the largest fraud amount (15,673,144.60). Rebalance staff toward West and Central offices; do not build region-specific collections playbooks from a 0.18pp late-rate spread. branch_segments.sql Support Resolution is 78.61% for Account Statement to 81.15% for Net Banking Issue; satisfaction stays 2.97-3.04 across issue types, and the Low income band resolves worst (78.36%). Fix the statement, KYC and loan-query workflows first, and investigate why satisfaction does not move with resolution - the driver looks systemic, not issue-specific. support_segments.sql

docs.title: Two entry points, one set of steps
docs.text:
Entry point Use Orchestrated by python main.py manual / CI full run, 10 gated steps in order human, make daily airflow/dags/banking_delta_daily.py scheduled production run (02:00 IST) Airflow scheduler

Both call the same scripts (scripts/run_jobs.py, scripts/run_*_tests.py, src/jobs/publish_marts.py) and the same SQL master loads (sql/{staging,analytics,marts}/00_master_load.sql). Airflow adds retries, pools, per-task state and alerting — it contains no pipeline logic of its own.

The 10 steps of main.py (python main.py --list):

1  sources    preflight         probe PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Databricks
2  raw        raw-inject        land MySQL, MongoDB, Databricks into raw
3  raw        raw-tests         DQ gate on raw
4  staging    staging-load      CALL staging.sp_load_all()
5  staging    staging-tests     DQ gate on staging
6  analytics  analytics-load    CALL analytics.sp_load_all()
7  analytics  analytics-tests   DQ gate on analytics
8  marts      marts-load        CALL marts.sp_load_all()
9  marts      marts-tests       DQ gate on marts
10 marts      publish           publish marts to Databricks Delta

docs.title: The Problem We Solved — Banking-Delta-Lakehouse
docs.text:
Business problem in one line: a bank's data lived in three disconnected systems, nobody agreed on a number, and decisions waited on manual reports — so we built one daily, audited pipeline that turns those systems into a single source of truth.

What was broken, how we approached it, how the design works, and what the three deliverable components (airflow/, dashboard/, reports/) do. The engineering blueprint is ../ARCHITECTURE.md.

Colour legend (same as ARCHITECTURE.md): blue = sources, violet = orchestration, orange = raw, cyan = staging, green = analytics / success, pink = marts, yellow = Delta, slate = audit, red = pain / DQ gates, indigo = consumers.

docs.title: 3. The approach
docs.text:
We did not start with dashboards. We made the data trustworthy first, then earned the right to serve it.

flowchart LR
    P1["1 · Discover<br/>inventory sources,<br/>agree the contract"] --> P2["2 · Land<br/>raw, as-is, replayable"]
    P2 --> P3["3 · Shape<br/>type · dedupe · SCD1"]
    P3 --> P4["4 · Model<br/>dim_* + fact_*"]
    P4 --> P5["5 · Serve<br/>business-shaped marts"]
    P5 --> P6["6 · Trust<br/>DQ gates · audit · orchestration"]

    classDef step fill:#e0e7ff,stroke:#4338ca,color:#312e81,stroke-width:2px
    classDef trust fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#15803d,color:#14532d,stroke-width:2px

    class P6 trust
  1. Discover — every source table got a JSON contract (columns, business key, load strategy) validated in CI, so an upstream schema change breaks the build, not a report.
  2. Land first — raw copies the source verbatim plus _batch_id/_loaded_at; anything downstream can be replayed from the original rows.
  3. Shape once, in SQL — staging procedures type, dedupe and keep current state.
  4. Model for questions — a star schema in analytics, business-shaped tables in marts.
  5. Gate everything — DQ suites run between layers; a critical failure blocks publish.
  6. Wrap with observability — audit tables, Airflow retries/alerts, a watchdog DAG.

docs.title: 4.1 Four layers, one owner each
docs.text:
Layer Answers Written by raw What did the source actually give us? the extractors (PySpark) staging Clean, current state of each entity? staging.sp_load_* analytics How do entities relate? (star schema) analytics.sp_load_* marts What does the business question look like? marts.sp_load_* Databricks Delta Where do consumers read? publish_marts.py

Only one writer may touch a schema, so two jobs can never fight over the same table.

Ten steps in order; a failing data-quality check stops the run before the next layer loads, so nothing downstream ever reads a half-loaded table.

  • 44 SQL checks across four suites (keys, bad dates, orphans, business rules, duplicates, completeness, reconciliation…), verdicts stored in audit.dq_*.
  • The gate commits its verdict, then raises — the reason for a failure survives the rollback.
  • A critical failure blocks publish: bad data never reaches the dashboard.

docs.title: 4.3 Crash-safe by construction: watermarks
docs.text:
The expensive bugs — duplicated or lost rows after a crash — are removed structurally: the data and its watermark move in one transaction, with optimistic locking so two concurrent runs cannot both win.

flowchart LR
    subgraph EXT["Extract · source → raw"]
        SRC[("source system")] -->|read only the new window| TMP[("raw._stg_table<br/>transient")]
        TMP -->|"ONE txn: promote + advance"| RAW[("raw.table")]
        RAW -.->|same txn| EW[("audit.extract_watermarks")]
        EW -.->|next window starts here| SRC
    end
    subgraph LOADC["Load · raw → staging"]
        RAW2[("raw.table")] -->|filter newer than watermark| STG2[("staging.table")]
        STG2 -.->|same block| TW[("audit.etl_watermarks")]
        TW -.->|next window starts here| RAW2
    end

    classDef src fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#1d4ed8,color:#1e3a8a,stroke-width:2px
    classDef raw fill:#ffedd5,stroke:#c2410c,color:#7c2d12,stroke-width:2px
    classDef staging fill:#cffafe,stroke:#0e7490,color:#164e63,stroke-width:2px

    class TMP,RAW,RAW2 raw
    class STG2 staging
    class EW,TW audit
  • Idempotent — re-running adds no duplicates (incremental layers dedupe on the business key; full loads TRUNCATE + INSERT atomically).
  • Crash-safe — a failure before commit leaves table and watermark untouched; the retry re-reads the same window.
  • Incremental — only the new slice of each source is read, so the run stays minutes.
  • Two watermark stores (source→raw, raw→staging) that are never mixed.

docs.title: 4.4 Everything is recorded
docs.text: Audit rows are written in their own transactions, so a FAILED record survives the data load's rollback: audit.pipeline_runs (one per execution), audit.table_runs (per attempt, with row counts), audit.pipeline_errors (classified, secret-redacted), audit.dq_run / dq_violation, and the two watermark tables. Runs always resolve to SUCCESS, PARTIAL or FAILED.

docs.title: airflow/ — when it runs and who it tells
docs.text:
Docker Compose stack (scheduler, worker, API server on :8080, Celery + Redis) with two DAGs — and no pipeline logic: it calls the same main.py entry points a human would.

  • banking_delta_daily — 02:00 IST, one active run, 5h timeout; loads retry once, DQ gates never retry (retries=0) because a data defect does not fix itself.
  • banking_watchdog — every 3 hours, reads audit.pipeline_runs, silent when healthy, mails [MISSED] / [STUCK] otherwise.
  • send_pipeline_summary emails [SUCCESS] / [FAILED] with the report PDF and .tex attached; fail_if_any_failed turns the run red so Airflow matches reality.

docs.title: dashboard/ — the read-only view
docs.text:
Streamlit + Plotly, six pages — Overview, KPI Explorer, Customers, Loans, Cards, Branches — each mapped to one mart.

  • Every chart is a live SELECT against Databricks Delta: no extracts, no cached copies; a 5-minute cache plus a manual refresh protect the warehouse.
  • Read-only credentials; runs locally (streamlit run app.py) or in Docker.

docs.title: reports/ — the paper trail
docs.text:
A LaTeX report builder (reports/chapters/, reports/scripts/build.py) producing three kinds: daily (verdict banner, KPI cards, checks), incident (one run, deep-dive) and weekly (digest).

  • Built as an Airflow task right after the run; PDF + .tex source are attached to the summary email, kept 30 days.
  • make report, report-incident RUN=<id>, report-weekly, report-fixture (no TeX, part of CI).

docs.title: 6. What the business gets
docs.text: Mart The question it answers mart_customer_360 Who is this customer across every product? mart_branch_performance How is each branch performing vs its peers? mart_monthly_transactions What is the transaction volume and value trend? mart_loan_portfolio What is the state of the loan book? mart_card_fraud Is card fraud increasing, and where? mart_support_performance Are tickets being resolved fast and well? mart_kpi_monthly The single set of monthly KPI numbers for leadership Before After Source of truth three systems, per-team extracts one warehouse, one governed mart layer Time to a new answer days of manual joining a query against a ready-made mart Reproducible? no — depends when you ran it yes — watermarks, batch ids, audit history Data quality found after publication 44 checks gate every layer, publish blocked Failure visibility stale dashboard, discovered late Airflow red, watchdog mails, report explains Trust "whose number is right?" "here is the run and the checks behind it"

docs.title: 7. Design decisions
docs.text: Decision Why Rejected Land verbatim into raw first replayable, auditable, no history lost transform straight from source PostgreSQL for transforms set-based procedures in one transaction Spark-side transforms Watermark advances with the data crash can neither lose nor double-count separate watermark update DQ gates between layers, commit-then-raise verdict survives; publish blocked validate after publish main.py and Airflow share one code path manual run reproduces the scheduled run Airflow-only logic — drifts fast NUMERIC(18,2) money, UTC timestamptz float rounds a balance off; UTC ends tz bugs float, server-local time Contracts validated in CI upstream change breaks the build, not a report discover at runtime Retry loads, never DQ gates infra fixes itself, data defects do not retry everything — hides defects

docs.title: 8. Guardrails
docs.text:
1. Watermarks advance only inside the load/extract transaction.
  2. Every load is safe to run twice with the same input.
  3. A critical DQ failure blocks publish.
  4. Each schema is written only by its owner.
  5. Money is NUMERIC(18,2); all instants are UTC.
  6. Audit rows survive failure (own transactions; commit before raise).
  7. Never weaken a test, hook or CI check to get green.

docs.title: Quick start — Banking-Delta-Lakehouse
docs.text: End-to-end guide to getting the pipeline running on a developer machine. For the full blueprint read ARCHITECTURE.md; for day-to-day operations read docs/RUNBOOK.md. Colour legend: docs/PIPELINE.md.

docs.title: 0. Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Git, uv, GNU Make (Windows: use tasks.bat, or install Make via Chocolatey)
  • Python 3.13 (pinned in pyproject.toml / .python-version)
  • Java 8/11/17/21 for the Spark extract paths
  • PostgreSQL 16 client (psql) and a disposable warehouse database
  • Docker + Docker Compose for the Airflow stack (optional but recommended)
  • A TeX distribution with latexmk + pdflatex for PDF reports (optional)

External services you must be able to reach: MySQL (banking_core_db), MongoDB (banking_support_db), Databricks workspace (SQL + Unity Catalog volume), and SMTP for alerts (optional).

docs.title: 1. Clone and configure
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/Nitinx12/Banking-Delta-Lakehouse.git
cd Banking-Delta-Lakehouse
cp .env.example .env          # Windows: copy .env.example .env

Edit .env with real credentials for PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Databricks, Spark, Airflow and SMTP. Never commit .env. The contract is enforced by tests/smoke/test_env_contract.py — every require()d variable must be present.

docs.title: 2. Install dependencies
docs.text:
make install        # uv sync --group dev
make hooks          # git config core.hooksPath .githooks  (mandatory)

On Windows without Make: tasks install then tasks hooks.

docs.title: 3. Verify the toolchain (no DB, no network)
docs.text:
make ci             # lint + contracts + sql-lint + coverage + smoke + report fixtures

This is the same gate CI runs. Fix any failure before continuing.

docs.title: 4. Bootstrap the PostgreSQL warehouse
docs.text:
Apply the ordered, idempotent scripts under sql/scripts/ (in numeric order, skipping 00_create_database if the DB already exists and 05_switch_* once the flip is done):

# disposable DB only
ALLOW_SQL_SMOKE=1 make sql-smoke

Then seed watermarks for the first incremental run of new tables (never for MySQL, which is full-load):

python scripts/seed_watermarks.py --dry-run
python scripts/seed_watermarks.py

docs.title: 4b. Land the bundled raw data (no source systems needed)
docs.text:
The repo ships gzipped CSV snapshots of all 10 source tables under data/raw/{mysql,mongo,databricks}/. If you cannot reach MySQL, MongoDB or Databricks, land them into raw instead (polars + COPY, one transaction per table, replace-snapshot semantics so a second run is safe):

make load-raw-csv                                # Windows: tasks load-raw-csv
make load-raw-csv ARGS="--dry-run"               # plan only, writes nothing
make load-raw-csv ARGS="--tables accounts"       # one table

Missing raw tables are created from contracts/<source>/<table>.json, so types match the project (money stays NUMERIC(18,2), never float). Continue with make staging && make dq-staging from here.

Maintainers refresh the snapshots with live source credentials (writes *.csv.gz in place):

make export-raw-csv

cd airflow
cp .env.airflow.example .env.airflow   # fill real secrets
docker compose --env-file .env.airflow up airflow-init   # must exit 0
docker compose --env-file .env.airflow up -d
# or from the repo root: make up / make down (adds dev bind mounts + GIT_SHA)

UI: http://127.0.0.1:8080. The DAGs are created paused — un-pause banking_delta_daily and banking_report_weekly deliberately.

python -m venv .venv && .venv\Scripts\activate   # or source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .streamlit/secrets.toml.example .streamlit/secrets.toml
streamlit run app.py                            # http://localhost:8501

The dashboard is read-only and shows only published Databricks marts.

Full gated run (writes to the warehouse and Databricks):

make daily          # or: python main.py

Single layer or step:

python main.py --list                  # show the 10 steps
python main.py --only staging-load
make staging && make dq-staging
make analytics && make dq-analytics

docs.title: Reporting: Banking Delta Lakehouse
docs.text:
Dynamic PDF reporting for the pipeline. When a run finishes, an alert fires or a digest is due, a Python builder reads the audit schema, scores what happened, renders LaTeX from Jinja templates, compiles reports/main.tex with pdfLaTeX and produces report.pdf. Airflow attaches the PDF to the summary mail. The report adapts to the news: a healthy night is a short verdict with a few charts, a bad night adds incident chapters, evidence and runbook pointers, and a serious one also produces a separate incident PDF.

Colour legend: docs/PIPELINE.md. Rules for agents in AGENTS.md always win on conflict; this page adds the reporting specific ones. Related: docs/AUDIT.md (data source), docs/AIRFLOW.md (DAG and mail), docs/RUNBOOK.md (actions linked from incidents), docs/TESTING.md (test tiers).

docs.title: 1. Goals and non goals
docs.text:
Goals:

  • Page one answers in ten seconds: is the pipeline healthy, what broke, what do I do next.
  • Fully dynamic: chapters, charts, flow colours and wording come from data, never from hand edited text. Any minor or major event changes the report.
  • One design system: Jinja for structure, LaTeX for typography, matplotlib for charts, TikZ for the pipeline flow.
  • Delivered by the existing Airflow summary mail as an attachment, with no new mail stack.
  • Reproducible: the same context.json always produces the same PDF.

Non goals:

  • It does not replace the DQ gates, the watchdog or the Streamlit dashboard.
  • It never changes pipeline state. It is a read only consumer of audit.* and the warehouse metadata.
  • It never shows row values, PII or credentials. Counts, names and statuses only, the same contract as audit_reader.py.
  • A failed report never turns a green pipeline run red.

docs.title: 3. Rules for agents
docs.text:
1. Read AGENTS.md, docs/AUDIT.md and sql/scripts/02_audit_tables.sql before writing a query. Use column names from the DDL, never from this page.
  2. Read only. The collector may SELECT from audit.*, the registry and MAX(_loaded_at) style freshness probes. No INSERT, UPDATE, CALL or DDL. Open the connection with default_transaction_read_only = on.
  3. No row values, PII, secrets or connection strings in context.json, charts, LaTeX or mail. Every free text field (error messages, violation messages) goes through the existing redaction (redact.py and src.utils.audit._redact) and is cut to 300 characters. Do not copy the regexes. If importing across packages is awkward, ask before promoting the helper to src/utils/redact.py.
  4. Every value that reaches LaTeX is escaped by the Jinja finalize hook (section 8). Raw LaTeX is allowed only through the explicit raw filter on values built by Python code, never on data from the warehouse.
  5. Compile with -no-shell-escape -halt-on-error. Never enable \write18 or --shell-escape, and never \input a path built from data.
  6. A missing or unknown state is never rendered as success. Same principle as summary.decide_status. Use UNKNOWN (grey) when a step has no audit evidence.
  7. The report derives status from audit.pipeline_runs, audit.table_runs, audit.dq_run and audit.pipeline_errors, never from Airflow task instances. The summary mail layers live Airflow states on top of the same audit rows (summary.collect_task_states, docs/AIRFLOW.md); the report stays audit only so both sides agree on pipeline facts.
  8. Do not "correct" timestamps. Times are shown as stored with their zone label, and the appendix links the open timezone offset issue (docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md, open issue 3).
  9. Thresholds and severity mappings live in reports/config/report.yaml. Lowering a severity or loosening a threshold needs a human decision, the same way DQ thresholds do.
  10. A report failure degrades, it does not block. Section failures render a visible "section unavailable" box, a compile failure retries in safe mode (section 10), and the Airflow task never sits in the failure gate.
  11. Output is deterministic. Sort every list, fix the random seed, set SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH from the run end time, never print now() inside the document body.
  12. Dependencies are added with uv only (uv add --group reports ...). No pip, no conda, no hand edited lock file.
  13. Style: one short header comment at the top of each file, no paragraph comments and no comments between code lines. SQL is uppercase keywords, one column per line, four space indent. Python passes ruff. Documentation prose uses no hyphens.
  14. Windows safe: pathlib, sys.executable, encoding="utf-8" on every open and read_text, no POSIX only calls, forward slashes inside LaTeX paths.
  15. Do not edit or import anything under reports/legacy/. It is reference material only.

docs.text:
Kind File Produced when Audience question daily report.pdf every banking_delta_daily run, always what happened last night incident incident.pdf any event with severity MAJOR or CRITICAL, plus watchdog alerts what broke, why, what now weekly weekly.pdf banking_report_weekly, Monday 08:00 Asia/Kolkata is the platform trending well

The incident PDF is produced in addition to report.pdf, so the daily report stays consistent every day. Both are attached to the same mail.

Chapter template Content Charts and visuals Included in 01_summary verdict banner, KPI cards, top events, next actions none, cards only all kinds 02_flow the 9 gated steps and 3 extracts as a coloured flow TikZ flow daily, incident 03_timeline task durations, retries, critical path task timeline daily, incident 04_volumes rows extracted and landed per table, deviation from trailing median volumes dumbbell, layer bars daily, weekly 05_dq DQ gate results per layer and check, violation counts DQ heatmap daily when any DQ row exists, incident, weekly 06_freshness table age against its window, watermark lag, last success age freshness bullet chart daily, weekly 07_incidents one block per MINOR or higher event with evidence and runbook link event table, error category bars when events exist 08_trends last N runs: duration, rows, failures, DQ failures small multiples weekly, daily appendix 09_appendix run metadata, full table run list, versions, known open issues, regeneration command tables all kinds

docs.title: 6. Events and severity
docs.text:
Every report starts from a list of events. An event is one fact about the run with a severity, a place and an impact.

Severity Meaning Verdict label Banner colour INFO normal, worth a line (for example a table skipped, no new data) HEALTHY green MINOR self healed or low impact (retry used, small deviation) ATTENTION amber MAJOR a gate or step failed, data late or partial ACTION REQUIRED red CRITICAL run failed, nothing published, or status unknown INCIDENT dark red

The run verdict is the maximum event severity, and its one-line headline and consequence come from wording: in report.yaml, one entry per severity. Mail subjects keep the existing [SUCCESS|WARNING|FAILED] marker from summary.py; the report verdict appears in the body and in the attachment file name, for example Banking-Delta_daily_20261021_ATTENTION.pdf.

docs.title: Rule catalogue
docs.text:
Rules live in reports/scripts/severity.py, one function per rule, each with a test.

Rule Signal (source) Condition Severity R001 audit.pipeline_runs.status FAILED CRITICAL R002 audit.pipeline_runs.status PARTIAL MAJOR R003 audit.dq_run a layer suite has status FAIL MAJOR R004 publish table_runs or DQ row_count_source_vs_published publish not SUCCESS, or published rows differ from source MAJOR R005 audit.pipeline_errors.error_category CONNECTION or SPARK on the final attempt MAJOR R006 audit.pipeline_errors.error_category CONCURRENCY that a retry resolved MINOR R007 audit.table_runs.attempt_number greater than 1 for any table MINOR R008 audit.data_quality_results WARNING severity check not passing MINOR R009 table_runs.rows_landed vs trailing median deviation above volume_deviation_ratio MINOR R010 full load table with zero rows landed always MAJOR R011 run duration vs trailing median above duration_regression_ratio MINOR R012 freshness from MAX(_loaded_at) and the contract window window exceeded contract severity (WARNING maps to MINOR, ERROR to MAJOR) R013 DQ schema_contract or contracts/ drift any violation MAJOR R014 watchdog [MISSED] or [STUCK] alert raised MAJOR R015 watchdog [WATCHDOG-ERROR] or a step with no audit evidence status unknown CRITICAL R016 collector section raised an error the section degraded MINOR R017 table_runs.status SKIPPED because no new data INFO R018 pipeline_runs counts vs the collected table_runs list any count disagrees with the tables MINOR

reports/scripts/collect.py builds one dictionary and writes data/context.json. Each section is collected in its own try block so one failure degrades only that section and is recorded in sections_failed (rule R016).

Query shapes (confirm the real names in the DDL first):

-- Shape only, parameterised. Never format values into SQL text.
SELECT
    status,
    total_tables,
    successful_tables,
    failed_tables,
    started_at,
    ended_at
FROM audit.pipeline_runs
WHERE dag_id = %(dag_id)s
  AND dag_run_id = %(dag_run_id)s;

FROM audit.table_runs

docs.text: data/fixtures/ holds synthetic contexts only, with invented table counts and no real values: healthy, minor_retry, major_dq_fail, critical_failed_run, weekly.
